config.title: Native Preferences & Secure Storage

intro.title: Native Preferences & Secure Storage
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple app that securely saves and retrieves user settings, like a theme preference, using native device storage. You'll learn how to use the Capacitor Preferences API for simple key-value storage and the Capacitor Secure Storage plugin for sensitive data. The core concept is interacting with native device storage through Ionic's Capacitor plugins. By the end, you'll understand how to persist data locally in a mobile app, choosing between simple and secure storage based on your data's needs.
intro.usecase: Native Preferences & Secure Storage are essential for mobile apps that need to persist user settings and sensitive data across sessions. In real products like banking apps, this pattern stores login tokens and account preferences securely. E-commerce apps use it to remember user addresses and payment methods between app launches. Social media apps rely on it to save user preferences for notifications and privacy settings, while fitness trackers store workout history and health data locally on the device.

objectives: Apply Ionic Native Preferences plugin to store simple key-value pairs in native storage
Implement secure storage capabilities using the Capacitor Preferences API for sensitive data
Define TypeScript interfaces to type-check data structures for native storage operations
Execute asynchronous methods to store data in native preferences with proper error handling
Retrieve stored values from native preferences and assign them to component variables
Utilize Angular services to encapsulate native storage logic and make it reusable
Construct reactive UI components that display data retrieved from native storage
Modify stored preferences in response to user interactions through form controls
Compare native preferences with secure storage to determine appropriate use cases
Handle storage errors and edge cases with try-catch blocks and user feedback
Access multiple stored values simultaneously using batch operations when available
Control data persistence by implementing clear and remove operations for stored preferences

steps.title: Import Ionic Angular core components
steps.instruction: Import the following Ionic UI components from '@ionic/angular/standalone': IonContent, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonList, IonItem, IonLabel, IonInput, IonButton, and IonToggle.
steps.hint: Use a single import statement with curly braces to import multiple components from the same package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing Ionic components
import { IonContent, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle } from '@ionic/angular/standalone';

steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for Ionic components is added to the file.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement from '@ionic/angular/standalone' with all the specified components.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Ionic UI components needed for building the interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've imported all the required components: IonContent, IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonList, IonItem, IonLabel, IonInput, IonButton, and IonToggle from '@ionic/angular/standalone'.

steps.title: Import Angular core modules
steps.instruction: Import CommonModule from '@angular/common' and FormsModule from '@angular/forms' in your component's imports array.
steps.hint: Add both imports to the imports array in your @Component decorator. These are standard Angular modules needed for common directives and form handling.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component should now have CommonModule and FormsModule imported and added to the imports array, enabling Angular's common directives and form features.
successCriteria: The code must include both CommonModule and FormsModule imported from their respective packages and added to the imports array in the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the Angular core modules needed for this lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported both CommonModule and FormsModule and added them to the imports array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've imported CommonModule from '@angular/common', FormsModule from '@angular/forms', and added both to the imports array in @Component.

steps.title: Import Capacitor Preferences plugin
steps.instruction: Import the Preferences plugin from '@capacitor/preferences' to enable native key-value storage capabilities in your app.
steps.hint: Add an import statement at the top of your file to bring in the Preferences API from the Capacitor plugin.
steps.analogousExample:
// Import the Preferences plugin
import { Preferences } from '@capacitor/preferences';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Preferences API from Capacitor is imported and available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The import statement for Preferences from '@capacitor/preferences' is correctly added to the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully imported the Capacitor Preferences plugin. This gives you access to native key-value storage APIs that work across iOS, Android, and web platforms.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing from the correct package '@capacitor/preferences' and using the correct export name 'Preferences'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement for the Capacitor Preferences plugin is missing or incorrect. You need to import { Preferences } from '@capacitor/preferences'.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a new component class named PreferencesDemoComponent with the @Component decorator. Set standalone: true and include the required imports array (CommonModule, FormsModule, and the listed Ionic components).
steps.hint: Define a new class with @Component decorator above it. The decorator should have selector, standalone, imports, and template properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new component class named PreferencesDemoComponent is created with the @Component decorator configured as specified.
successCriteria: The code should contain a new class named PreferencesDemoComponent with @Component decorator having selector, standalone: true, imports array with the listed modules/components, and a template property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the PreferencesDemoComponent with the correct decorator configuration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that all required properties are present in the @Component decorator: selector, standalone: true, imports array, and template.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Make sure you define a class named PreferencesDemoComponent with the @Component decorator configured as specified.

steps.title: Initialize component state
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent class, add three properties: username as a string initialized to an empty string, notificationsEnabled as a boolean initialized to false, and storageResult as a string initialized to an empty string.
steps.hint: Add these properties directly in the class body, using TypeScript type annotations and initial values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class now has three typed properties with initial values to store app state.
successCriteria: The AppComponent class contains three properties: username (string, initialized to ''), notificationsEnabled (boolean, initialized to false), and storageResult (string, initialized to '').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the component state with three typed properties. This gives us variables to store user preferences and storage operation results.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but some properties are missing or not correctly typed/initialized. Make sure you have all three: username (string = ''), notificationsEnabled (boolean = false), and storageResult (string = '').
steps.feedbackWrong: The component state properties aren't set up correctly. You need to add three properties inside the AppComponent class with proper TypeScript types and initial values.

steps.title: Create savePreferences handler
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent class, create an async method named savePreferences that will handle saving the component's state values to native storage.
steps.hint: Define an async method with the name savePreferences. You can leave the implementation empty for now or add a console.log to verify it's being called.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent class will have an async savePreferences method defined, ready to be implemented with storage logic in the next steps.
successCriteria: The component contains an async method named savePreferences that returns a Promise<void>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the savePreferences method. This method will serve as the handler for saving user preferences to native storage.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the method is async and named exactly 'savePreferences'. Check that it's defined inside the AppComponent class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The savePreferences method wasn't created correctly. Make sure to define an async method with the exact name 'savePreferences' inside the AppComponent class.

steps.title: Create loadPreferences handler
steps.instruction: Inside the AppComponent class, create an async method called loadPreferences that will retrieve stored values using Capacitor's Preferences plugin.
steps.hint: Define a method with the async keyword and use Preferences.get() to fetch stored values. You'll need to handle the returned values and update component properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent class will have a loadPreferences method that uses Preferences.get() to retrieve stored values.
successCriteria: The code should include an async method named loadPreferences that uses Preferences.get() to fetch stored values for 'username' and 'notificationsEnabled' keys.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the loadPreferences method. This method will retrieve stored preferences using Capacitor's Preferences plugin.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your method is async and uses Preferences.get() to retrieve values for both 'username' and 'notificationsEnabled' keys.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loadPreferences method is missing or incomplete. Remember to create an async method that uses Preferences.get() to retrieve stored values.

steps.title: Create clearPreferences handler
steps.instruction: Create an async method named clearPreferences() that uses Preferences.clear() to remove all stored preferences and updates storageResult to indicate success.
steps.hint: Add a new async method inside the AppComponent class that calls Preferences.clear() and sets this.storageResult to a success message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppComponent will have a clearPreferences() method that clears all stored preferences using the Capacitor Preferences plugin and updates the storageResult property.
successCriteria: The method must be async, call Preferences.clear(), and update this.storageResult with a success message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the clearPreferences handler. This method will clear all stored preferences when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your method is async, calls Preferences.clear(), and updates this.storageResult with a success message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The clearPreferences method should be async, call Preferences.clear(), and update this.storageResult. Check the syntax and make sure you're using the correct plugin method.

steps.title: Add basic component template structure
steps.instruction: Replace the existing template with a basic Ionic structure containing an IonHeader with IonToolbar and IonTitle set to 'Preferences Demo', and an IonContent area.
steps.hint: Use the Ionic components IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, and IonContent to create the basic page layout.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of basic Ionic template structure
@Component({
  selector: 'app-example',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent],
  template: `
    <ion-header>
      <ion-toolbar>
        <ion-title>Example App</ion-title>
      </ion-toolbar>
    </ion-header>
    <ion-content>
      <!-- Content will go here -->
    </ion-content>
  `
})
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a proper Ionic page structure with a header toolbar containing the title 'Preferences Demo' and a content area ready for UI elements.
successCriteria: The template should contain exactly one ion-header with ion-toolbar and ion-title set to 'Preferences Demo', and one ion-content element. The existing 'Hello World' paragraph should be removed.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the basic Ionic template structure with a header and content area. This provides the foundation for building the rest of the UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the template structure needs adjustment. Make sure you have exactly one ion-header containing an ion-toolbar with an ion-title set to 'Preferences Demo', and one ion-content element. The 'Hello World' paragraph should be removed.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template structure doesn't match the requirements. You need to replace the existing template with Ionic components: ion-header with ion-toolbar and ion-title set to 'Preferences Demo', and ion-content.

steps.title: Add input for username
steps.instruction: Inside the IonContent in your template, add an IonItem with an IonLabel that says 'Username:' and an IonInput with two-way data binding to the username property using [(ngModel)]='username'.
steps.hint: Use Ionic form components: IonItem, IonLabel, and IonInput. Remember to bind the input to the component's username property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of an Ionic form input with two-way binding
<IonItem>
  <IonLabel>Username:</IonLabel>
  <IonInput [(ngModel)]="username"></IonInput>
</IonItem>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now includes a form input field for the username that is bound to the component's username property.
successCriteria: The template should contain an IonItem with IonLabel and IonInput elements, and the IonInput should have [(ngModel)]='username' for two-way data binding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added an input field for the username with proper data binding.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both IonLabel and IonInput inside IonItem, and that the IonInput uses [(ngModel)]='username'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input field for username is missing or incorrect. Please add IonItem with IonLabel and IonInput with two-way binding to the username property.

steps.title: Add toggle for notifications
steps.instruction: Add an IonItem with an IonLabel 'Enable Notifications:' and an IonToggle bound to the notificationsEnabled property using [(ngModel)].
steps.hint: Use the IonItem, IonLabel, and IonToggle components from Ionic Angular. The IonToggle should be inside the IonItem and use two-way binding with notificationsEnabled.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Example of an IonItem with IonToggle -->
<IonItem>
  <IonLabel>Enable Feature</IonLabel>
  <IonToggle [(ngModel)]="isFeatureEnabled"></IonToggle>
</IonItem>
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will include an Ionic toggle control for enabling/disabling notifications, bound to the notificationsEnabled property.
successCriteria: The code must include IonItem with IonLabel containing 'Enable Notifications:' and an IonToggle with [(ngModel)]='notificationsEnabled'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a toggle control for notifications that's properly bound to the notificationsEnabled property.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both IonLabel with the correct text and IonToggle with two-way binding [(ngModel)]='notificationsEnabled'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle control isn't properly configured. Check that you're using IonItem, IonLabel with 'Enable Notifications:', and IonToggle with [(ngModel)]='notificationsEnabled'.

steps.hint: Use the Ionic Button component with click handlers. The savePreferences handler is already defined, but loadPreferences and clearPreferences need to be added. Display storageResult in a paragraph.

successCriteria: The template must include three IonButton elements with (click) handlers for savePreferences, loadPreferences, and clearPreferences, and a paragraph element that displays storageResult.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the action buttons and display area. The buttons are wired to their respective handlers, and the storage result is displayed.
